extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties in PTAB inter partes review proceedings (petitioners, patent owners, counsel, expert witnesses)
extracted.subtask_description: A Patent Trial and Appeal Board Final Written Decision resolving instituted inter partes review grounds (claim construction, obviousness over references, evidentiary motions) and ordering claims unpatentable or not. Focuses on legal standards and evidentiary burdens applicable in IPRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for unpatentability in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner must show unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence (see 35 U.S.C. § 316(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board determines whether Petitioner has shown by a preponderance that each challenged claim is unpatentable; claims not shown by a preponderance are sustained. Example: claims 1–6, 10, 11, 14, 17, 19, and 20 were found unpatentable by a preponderance; claim 18 was not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard in IPR (broadest reasonable construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an inter partes review, the Board interprets claim terms in an unexpired patent according to the broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification of the patent in which they appear (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Cuozzo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent any special definitions, give claim terms their ordinary and customary meaning as would be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention. Any special definitions must be set forth with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision (In re Paulsen). Only terms in controversy need be construed, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Vivid Techs.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended claim language 'comprising' (inclusion of unrecited ingredients)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the term 'comprising' permits inclusion of elements in addition to those specified in the claims (In re Baxter; CIAS, Inc. v. Alliance Gaming Corp.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a formulation is recited with 'comprising' and a property is attributed to 'the formulation,' the broadest reasonable construction can include embodiments containing additional, unrecited ingredient(s) that may contribute to the claimed functional property. Example applied: the formulation 'inhibits aggregation' may include additional unrecited ingredients that cause inhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of functional claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A functional limitation attributing a property to 'the formulation' is read as a property of the formulation as a whole, not necessarily attributable to any particular recited ingredient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not read a functional property as requiring that a specific recited ingredient (e.g., the aluminum salt) itself perform the function unless the claim language or clear specification text requires it. The property may be satisfied by the combination of recited elements or by additional, unrecited elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to import limitations from the specification into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not import limitations from the specification into claims absent clear support; claims are not limited to examples or measurements described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: although the specification measures inhibition of aggregation by antigenicity in Example 4, the Board refused to read an 'antigenicity' limitation into the claim because the claim does not require a specific level of immunogenicity and the presence of a polysaccharide-protein conjugate already supplies the immunogenic element. Use specification to inform ordinary meaning but not to add unclaimed numerical or functional thresholds unless claim language requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (factual determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of ordinary skill in the art is a factual determination that provides a primary guarantee of objectivity in an obviousness analysis (Graham factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the skill level using objective indicia (education, degrees, years of experience, relevant technical experience). The Board may adopt a party's proposed definition or a hybrid if record evidence supports it. Expert qualifications are recognized, but the weight of their testimony depends on supporting facts and data; opinions without disclosed underlying facts/data may be given little or no weight (Office Patent Trial Practice Guide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness framework (Graham factors and KSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The obviousness inquiry is resolved based on (1) scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art, (3) level of ordinary skill in the art, and (4) secondary considerations, and requires a reason to combine with a reasonable expectation of success (Graham; KSR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is unpatentable if, as a whole, it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill. Mere knowledge of separate elements in the prior art is insufficient; there must be an articulated reason a skilled artisan would combine the references and a reasonable expectation that the combination would work. Avoid hindsight—using the inventor's disclosure as a blueprint to piece together prior art is improper (KSR; In re Fine; Kinetic Concepts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason to combine and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: To support an obviousness combination, a party must show a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill to combine the prior art references and a reasonable expectation that the combination would succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculative theoretical concerns or unsupported assertions do not suffice. Affirmative evidence (teachings in the references, expert testimony grounded in facts, or common general knowledge) must support both the motivation to combine and the expectation of successful combination. The Board will reject hindsight-tinged 'natural progression' arguments absent specific evidentiary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in obviousness and modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: A feature that is the necessary and inevitable result of applying the prior art combination may be inherent, but inherency must be established by clear evidence, not just speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting that a combined reference inherently produces a claimed property (e.g., inhibition of silicone-induced aggregation), the petitioner must show that the property necessarily flows from the combination, supported by evidence or sound expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia / secondary considerations of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence such as commercial success, industry praise, long-felt but unsolved need, copying by others, and overcoming failures of others may weigh against obviousness if a nexus to the claimed invention is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations must be timely raised and supported by admissible evidence showing a nexus to the claimed features. The Board may decline to reach or give weight to secondary considerations if the petitioner has not first established obviousness or if the necessary evidentiary predicate is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and weight of evidence and expert testimony in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions to exclude are governed by rules of evidence considerations, but the Board often treats disputes about expert testimony and its bases as matters of weight rather than admissibility; the moving party bears the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although parties may cite FRE 702/703, the Board (composed of technically competent judges) assesses expert testimony credibility and weight; testimony offered without underlying facts/data may be given little or no weight. Timeliness, relevance, authentication, hearsay concerns, and compliance with page limits may render submissions moot or grounds for exclusion if relied upon; but if the Board does not rely on such exhibits, exclusion motions may be dismissed as moot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and disposition on motions to exclude in PTAB practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The moving party has the burden to establish entitlement to exclusion; the Board will dismiss motions as moot when it does not rely on the contested evidence, and deny motions when issues go to weight rather than admissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example outcomes: exhibits tied to secondary considerations were deemed moot when the Board did not reach that issue; expert declaration portions challenging state-of-the-art went to probative weight and were not excluded. The Board may permit limited use of evidence (e.g., for assessing a witness's qualifications) while rejecting its use for proving prior art status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of institution-stage findings and record in final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary determinations (e.g., in an Institution Decision) may inform the final decision but are subject to revision based on the full evidentiary record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may have adopted a preliminary skill-in-the-art description at institution but will revisit and refine that description upon consideration of the full record, including expert declarations and prior art submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for concrete evidence when asserting obviousness of complex, multicomponent inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims reciting many structural elements (e.g., a 13‑valent conjugate composition), a petitioner must provide evidence that the prior art taught or would have led a skilled artisan to make those specific combinations with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions of a 'natural progression' from smaller to larger valency vaccines are insufficient without evidence that the specific multivalent composition was taught, tested, or would have been expected to work. The Board expects documentation (publications, studies, or convincing expert testimony with factual basis) showing that the exact multi-component arrangement was known or would have been predictably achievable.
